query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the overall wear resistance of a FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coating is controlled by the in‐situ formation of a continuous and adherent oxide scale at the coating surface. This oxide layer increases hardness and reduces plastic deformation during sliding contact, thereby lowering wear rates.
generation.material_initial_state: A sputter-deposited, homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu coating (amorphous or nanocrystalline) on a conventional metal substrate with minimal pre‐oxidation.
generation.intervention: Expose the coating to a high-temperature, oxidizing environment (e.g., 600–800°C) under controlled sliding wear conditions to promote the formation of a protective oxide layer, compared to a baseline test conducted at room temperature or in an inert atmosphere (minimal oxidation).
generation.conditions: Wear tests under cyclic sliding at elevated temperatures (600–800°C) with defined normal loads representative of high-temperature applications. The atmosphere should be controlled to ensure oxidation in the test group versus inert conditions in the control.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a continuous oxide scale (e.g., chromium oxide and possibly mixed Cu oxide phases) at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the reactive elements (especially Cr) in the alloy preferentially oxidize, forming a hard and adherent oxide layer. This layer acts as a diffusion barrier and reduces direct mechanical contact between the sliding bodies, thereby limiting plastic deformation and material removal (wear) under high-load conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, coatings exposed to the high-temperature oxidizing environment will form a uniform oxide layer that results in a lower wear rate and reduced coefficient of friction compared to the baseline (room temperature or inert atmosphere) coating with little or no oxide formation.
generation.baseline: A FeNiCrCoCu coating exhibiting its initial homogeneous, unoxidized microstructure and tested at room temperature or in an inert atmosphere where oxidation is suppressed.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to be valid in the temperature range of 600–800°C under wear loads typical of high-temperature applications. Outside this range (e.g., very low or extremely high temperatures) or under drastically different loading conditions, other wear mechanisms might dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise composition, thickness, and adhesion quality of the oxide scale required for optimal wear resistance remain uncertain, as do the kinetics of oxide formation relative to the abrasion rate during sliding wear.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings. Age one set at 600–800°C in an oxidizing atmosphere to deliberately form the oxide layer, and age the second set under the same thermal and load conditions but in an inert (oxygen‐free) atmosphere to suppress oxidation. Then, subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under high-temperature conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or depth of wear tracks)
Surface analysis of oxide composition and thickness using XPS/SEM
Microstructural characterization (TEM/AFM) of the worn surfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidized coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or lower friction compared to the inert-aged coatings—or if no continuous oxide layer is observed on the oxidized samples—the hypothesis that the protective oxide scale governs high-temperature wear resistance would be falsified.

The nanoindentation technique has been extensively adopted to investigate the mechanical properties of solids with a small size. It has also been used for investigating the creep behavior of MPEAs at both ambient and elevated temperatures. Ma et al. [] studied the creep behavior of face-centered-cubic (FCC) and body-centered-cubic (BCC) MPEA thin films at room temperature. They pointed out that creep strain of the FCC CoCrFeNiCu MPEA thin film increased by enhancing the holding load or loading rate, while a BCC CoCrFeNiCuAl2.5 MPEA thin film showed a better creep resistance. The creep behavior of grains with different orientations was studied in a single-phase FCC FeCoNiCrMn MPEA from room temperature to 600 °C in our previous study []. The dislocation-climb mechanism was dominant in both {111} and {100} planes, the hardest and the softest orientation, respectively. It is likely that the deformation kinetics in FCC structures could differ from those in BCC structures. It is, therefore, of interest to evaluate the creep behavior of the grains with the strongest nature, i.e., the {110} plane, in a BCC MPEA. Another issue that can arise is the local formation of voids, pores, or gaps between adjacent grains and cracks forming perpendicular to the substrate surface, which also affect the apparent nanoindentation measurement value at or near that feature and result in a misleading data point. As a practical matter, when measuring dozens to hundreds of unique composition locations as may be necessary when concentrations of four or more elements are simultaneously varying across a combinatorial material library, only a limited number of nanoindentation repetitions, for instance, 3–5, can be made at each location. Identifying and handling data points that might be outliers becomes time-consuming and difficult, and it is effectively impossible to reliably distinguish which ones are actually measurement failures.
